**The Weight of Silence**

The first time I understood the weight of silence, I was twelve years old, sitting on the edge of my bed with a half-eaten bag of potato chips and a comic book I’d already read three times. My mother was in the kitchen, her voice low and steady, talking to someone on the phone—someone who wasn’t me. I could hear the murmur of her words, the occasional laugh, the way her tone shifted when she thought I wasn’t listening. But I was. Always listening.

That night, she hung up and came into my room without a word. She sat on the bed beside me, her fingers brushing against the comic’s cover like she was testing the air for something. Then she said, *"Your father’s not coming back."*

I remember the way the words settled in my chest, heavy as a stone. Not because they were unexpected—my parents had been fighting for months, their arguments sharp and quiet, like knives wrapped in cloth—but because of the silence that followed. No explanation. No apology. Just the two of us, sitting there, the weight of what wasn’t said pressing down on us both.

I learned that night that silence isn’t the absence of sound. It’s the absence of truth. It’s the space where things go unspoken, where wounds fester because no one has the courage—or the words—to name them.

---

Years later, I found myself in a café in Paris, staring at a steaming cup of coffee I hadn’t touched. Across from me, my best friend, Claire, was talking about her new job, her voice bright and unburdened. She was telling me about the promotion, the new team, the way her boss had clapped her on the back and said, *"You’re the one we want."* I should have been happy for her. Instead, I was thinking about the last time we’d spoken—really spoken—not about work or weather or the latest scandal on social media, but about the way her eyes had gone dark when she said, *"I don’t know if I can do this anymore."*

I had nodded and changed the subject.

Silence had won again.

---

There’s a kind of violence in silence. Not the kind that shouts or slams doors, but the kind that erodes. It’s the unanswered question, the unspoken fear, the love that goes unsaid until it’s too late. My father left because he couldn’t bear the weight of his own words. My mother never told me why she stayed. Claire and I both pretended everything was fine because the alternative was too heavy.

We are all, in some way, complicit in the silence. We choose it. We let it grow between us like an untrimmed hedge, thick and impenetrable, until the only way to cross it is to force a path through the thorns.

---

I think about this often now, sitting in my small apartment, the city humming outside my window. I have a job I tolerate, friends I see when I can, a life that looks, from the outside, like it’s going somewhere. But sometimes, in the quiet moments—when the TV is off, when the phone isn’t buzzing, when no one is asking me how I am—I wonder if I’ve spent too much time letting silence define me.

What if I started speaking? Not just the small talk, the polite exchanges, the words that fill the air but mean nothing. What if I said the things that matter? The fears, the doubts, the quiet desperation that sometimes grips me when I think about how little I really know, how much I’ve let go unsaid.

There’s a risk in that, of course. Vulnerability is dangerous. People might not like what they hear. They might walk away. But what’s worse than that? A life where the only sound is the echo of what we never dared to say.

---

I don’t know if I’ll ever be brave enough to break the silence completely. Some habits run too deep. Some fears are too old. But I can try. I can start small.

Today, I’ll ask Claire how she’s really doing. Not about her job, not about the weather, but about the way her hands tremble when she’s tired, the way she sometimes looks at me like she’s waiting for something she doesn’t know how to ask for.

Maybe tomorrow, I’ll tell my mother that I still miss my father. That I don’t blame her. That I just wish, sometimes, she’d let me in.

And maybe, just maybe, the silence won’t feel so heavy anymore.

---

The words are out there now, floating in the air between us, waiting to be spoken. The question is whether we’ll let them stay silent—or whether we’ll finally give them voice.

Because silence is a choice. And so is speaking. And if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that the things we don’t say have a way of haunting us long after we’ve stopped listening.
